newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kohl sees "active" Yeltsin resolving NATO issue.
newsitem.headline: Kohl sees "active" Yeltsin resolving NATO issue.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said Russian President Boris Yeltsin, who faces heart surgery this month, was "fully active" during talks near Moscow on Saturday and promised to help settle the dispute over NATO enlargement.
"President Yeltsin was fully active throughout these discussions," Kohl, who describes himself as a personal friend, told reporters before flying home after a seven-hour visit.
"Of course you can see that he is facing a serious operation. He knows this and talks about it."
Kohl said Yeltsin, with whom he strolled and took a boat trip at the president's hunting lodge after four hours of talks, confirmed he would undergo an operation at the end of the month in Moscow.
"Boris Yeltsin is very optimistic that this procedure, which is essential...will be successful," Kohl added. He declined to give his own opinion about Yeltsin's chances of recovery.

Once he was restored to health, the 65-year-old president had agreed to play a "very active" part in negotiations to resolve differences between Moscow and the North Atlantic defence alliance over NATO's plans to admit former Soviet-bloc countries in central and eastern Europe.

"It's a complex situation for reasons everyone here knows, but we are both of the opinion...that this subject should be brought to a conclusion in 1997," Kohl said, stressing that the issue should be resolved without creating new fears.
Kohl said there should be high-level talks with those central and east European states who want to join NATO.
"At the end of this year or the start of next, real discussions will begin," he said.
The chancellor said he had passed on good wishes from other world leaders he had talked to in recent days, including French President Jacques Chirac and U.S. President Bill Clinton.
Kohl said the leaders of the Group of Seven industrial powers wanted to see a definite end to the war in Chechnya, where Yeltsin's envoy, Alexander Lebed, agreed a peace deal last week.
The chancellor declined to be drawn into speculation about a power struggle in the Kremlin as Yeltsin faces surgery, but said the president did not strike him as someone who was about to lose power.
The two men discussed who would control Russia's nuclear arsenal while Yeltsin was on the operating table. But Kohl said he would not reveal the content of that part of the talks.
